bodyHtml:
Here are some words in the Khalkha dialect of Mongolian, a language spoken by approximately 5.2 million people in Mongolia and parts of China. Normally, Mongolian is written in either the Cyrillic or native Mongolian script. However, for ease of reading, all words have been transcribed into Latin script.

For each word, the singular, plural, and directive1 forms are given, as well as the pronunciation of the singular form. Some forms are missing.

Note: in the Pronunciation column, a colon (:) after a vowel marks vowel length. ´ over a vowel marks stress. [ɢ] denotes a consonant that sounds like the g of green, pronounced farther back in the mouth. [ŋ] denotes the ng sound of sing.

1. The directive case has the meaning of movement towards something. For example, havčaarluu, the directive case of “dog”, means “towards the dog.”

F1. Fill in the missing forms (1-10) in the table above.

F2. One of the following Mongolian words was originally a loanword from another language: nutag, künda, šoron, gudamž, ehner. Which one is it?

F3. Give the plural, directive, and pronunciation of the following words:

A) haančlah
‘king’
B) gürvel
‘lizard’

‘store’

questions.partPrompt: Fill in the missing forms (1-10) in the table.
One of the following Mongolian words was originally a loanword from another language: nutag, kunda, soron, gudamz, ehner (as printed: nutag, künda, šoron, gudamž, ehner). Which one is it?
Give the plural, directive, and pronunciation of each of the following words: A) haančlah 'king', B) gürvel 'lizard', C) delgüür 'store', D) zuun 'century', E) čanar 'quality'.

hints.text: Sort the singular words into two groups by the vowels they contain: one group uses a, o, u and the other uses e, ö, ü. Then look at which shape of ending each group takes. The endings come in matched pairs, such as -uud next to -üüd.

There are three different plural endings, and the choice depends on the stem: nouns naming people take one ending, stems that end in a vowel take another, and the rest take a third. The directive ending also has two shapes (one starting with l, one starting with r) and which you get depends on the last sound of the stem. For pronunciation, compare each spelling with its transcription letter by letter: h, g, final n, u and ü each behave regularly, and the stress mark always lands in a predictable place relative to long vowels.

Take heer 'field', which is not one of the words you must fill in. Its vowels are e, so all its endings use the front shapes: plural heerüüd, not heeruud. It ends in r, and every stem in the data ending in r takes the l-shaped directive (compare havčaarluu, mangarluu, sugarluu), which gives heerlüü. Its pronunciation [xé:r] shows three regular facts at once: written h is said as x, written ee is a single long vowel, and the stress sits on that long vowel.

explanationHtml:
What the columns are telling you

Every row gives one noun in three forms (singular, plural, directive — the case meaning “towards X”) plus a pronunciation of the singular. So there are really three little systems to crack: how the plural ending is chosen, how the directive ending is chosen, and how spelling maps onto pronunciation.

Step 1: vowel harmony (the reason for the title)

Line up the endings and you see they always come in pairs: -uud / -üüd, -čuud / -čüüd, -luu / -lüü, -ruu / -rüü. Which member you get depends on the vowels already in the stem:

  • Back words (containing a, o, u) take the u-endings: havčaaruud, zutanruu, galruu, nuguučuud.
  • Front words (containing e, ö, ü) take the ü-endings: örhüüd, heerlüü, denlüüčüüd, gölögrüü.

Crucially, no single word in the table mixes the two sets. That is what “vowel harmony” means: all the vowels of a word belong to one team.

Step 2: choosing the plural ending

Three plural endings show up:

  • nar (a separate word) for nouns naming people: mangar nar ‘fools’, hun nar ‘men’, aav nar ‘fathers’, hüühen nar ‘women’. So ‘husband’ gives nökör nar and ‘king’ gives haančlah nar.
  • -čuud / -čüüd after a stem that ends in a vowel: denlüüčüüd, nuguučuud, and therefore darga gives dargačuud (printed dargachuud in the official key).
  • -uud / -üüd for everything else, i.e. non-human nouns ending in a consonant: övsüüd, negüüd, zutanuud, galuud. So šüleg gives šülegüüd (front) and ovog gives ovoguud (back), while zuun gives zuunuud and čanar gives čanaruud.

Step 3: choosing the directive ending

Compare the last sound of the stem with the consonant of the ending:

  • stem ends in r: the ending starts with l — havčaarluu, mangarluu, sugarluu, heerlüü, nökörlüü. That is why ‘store’ gives delgüürlüü and ‘quality’ gives čanarluu.
  • anything else (including l, g, h, n, s, v and vowels): the ending starts with r — galruu, örhrüü, övsrüü, hunruu, gölögrüü, nuguuruu. So neg gives negruu, šüleg gives šülegrüü, darga gives dargaruu, ovog gives ovogruu, gürvel gives güvelrüü-style gürvelrüü, zuun gives zuunruu, and haančlah gives haančlahruu.

Step 4: from spelling to pronunciation

Match each spelling against its transcription and the rules fall out:

  • h is [x]: havčaar is [xavčá:r], örh is [ɵ́rx], hüühen is [xú:xeŋ].
  • doubled vowel = one long vowel, marked with a colon: heer is [xé:r], aav is [á:v].
  • stress falls on the first long vowel; if there is no long vowel, on the first syllable. havčaar [xavčá:r] has stress on the second syllable because that is where the long vowel is, while mangar [mánɢar] has no long vowel and stresses the first.
  • g is pronounced further back ([ɢ]) in back words but stays [g] in front words: gal [ɢál], sugar [sʊ́ɢar], ovog [óvoɢ], versus neg [nég], šüleg [šúleg].
  • word-final n is [ŋ]: hun [xʊ́ŋ], zutan [zʊ́taŋ], hüühen [xú:xeŋ].
  • written u is [ʊ] (back), written ü is [u] (front): nuguu [nʊɢʊ́:] versus denlüü [denlú:].

Put those together: darga has no long vowel, so stress is on the first syllable, and g in a back word is [ɢ] — giving [dárɢa]. zuun has long back uu and a final n — [zʊ́:ŋ]. delgüür has its long vowel in the second syllable — [delgú:r]. gürvel is a front word with no long vowel — [gúrvel]. čanar — [čánar]. haančlah begins with a long a and ends in h — [xá:nčlax].

Step 5: spotting the loanword

Native Mongolian words obey vowel harmony, so a word that mixes front and back vowels is a suspect. Test each candidate: nutag (u, a — all back), šoron (o, o — back), gudamž (u, a — back), ehner (e, e — front). Only künda pairs a front ü with a back a, breaking harmony — so that is the borrowed word.
_reviewNotes:
Please verify the exact IPA symbols I transcribed in the Pronunciation column of the data table; the scan is ambiguous for three cells: mangar (transcribed [mánɢar] - could be [máŋɢar]), nökör ([nékər] - possibly [nɵ́kɵr]) and gölög ([gélɵg] - possibly [gɵ́lɵg]). These body cells are not graded.
The official solution lists only F1 items 1-8; it gives no answers for blanks (9) and (10) (plural and directive of ovog). Keys F1.9 = ovoguud and F1.10 = ovogruu are MY OWN derivation and must be verified.
The official solution's F3 table row for haančlah is corrupted: its Directive cell repeats 'haančlah' and its Pronunciation cell reads '[xavčá:r]' (both leftovers from the problem table), and the Translation column of the whole solution table repeats 'dog/household/fool' from the problem. I used the official plural (haančlah nar) but supplied F3.2 = haančlahruu and F3.3 = [xá:nčlax] myself - UNOFFICIAL, verify.
F1.6: the solution prints 'dargachuud' with ch although the data uses č; I kept the solution spelling as the key and accept 'dargačuud'.
F3.4: the official key is gürvelčüüd, which conflicts with gal > galuud in the data; I added 'gürvelüüd' as an accepted variant.
Points were split evenly within parts (F1 = 4, F2 = 1, F3 = 5); no official per-item breakdown was given.
